title: The Company Building You Can Read Without Entering
concept: Every organisation's internet infrastructure is like a large building — and DNS is the building's public information directory. Each DNS record type is a different section of that directory. The organisation wrote every entry themselves. All of it is publicly readable. None of it requires permission to access.
anchor: DNS records are the building directory: A = front door address. MX = mail room. NS = management office. TXT = notice board. CNAME = forwarding sign. PTR = reverse directory. SRV = services catalog. An investigator who reads every section of the directory before entering the building always arrives knowing more than the building expected.
explanation:
Picture a large corporate office building. Before you enter, there is a public information directory in the lobby that anyone can read. It lists:

— The building's street address (A record)
— Where the mail room is located (MX record)
— Which office manages the official building records (NS record)
— The notice board with posted announcements, security certifications, and vendor relationships (TXT record)
— A forwarding sign: 'For payroll services, proceed to Annex Building B on Oak Street' (CNAME record)
— The reverse directory: cross-reference a room number to find whose office it is (PTR record)
— The services catalog: 'Legal consultation available at Suite 405, Room 12' (SRV record)

Now imagine that the organisation wrote every entry in this directory themselves. They added each one because a specific service needed it to function. They never thought about who else might read it.

DNS enumeration is reading the entire directory before deciding where to go — which door to knock on, which department to investigate, which annex building might be less well-guarded than the headquarters. The organisation gave you the map. You are simply learning to read it.

meanings: Every record type tells a different story — A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, CNAME, PTR, SRV are eight different intelligence sources
Nameservers are the authoritative source — always query them directly for zone transfer attempts
Uncover subdomains systematically — the forgotten branches are often the most exposed
Map the complete infrastructure before touching anything — DNS gives you the blueprint before active scanning begins
